items.stem: A town recreation department wants to estimate the fraction of all town residents who use public parks at least once per week. Which of the following sampling methods best supports a conclusion about all town residents?
choices: Survey the first 100 people who call the recreation department on a weekday
Survey 100 people who are using the largest public park on a Saturday
Survey 100 residents who volunteer to respond to a post on the department's social-media page
Randomly select 100 names from a complete list of all town residents and survey those people
items.explanation: Randomly selecting names from a complete list gives each resident an opportunity to be selected and is most likely to produce a representative sample. The other methods may overrepresent people who use parks, use social media, or contact the department.

per_choice.correct: Randomly selecting names from a complete list gives each resident an opportunity to be selected and is most likely to produce a representative sample. The other methods may overrepresent people who use parks, use social media, or contact the department.
per_choice.trap: Choosing the largest sample location as representative produces the second choice by assuming park visitors represent all residents.

items.trap: Choosing the largest sample location as representative produces the second choice by assuming park visitors represent all residents.

items.stem: A restaurant manager randomly selects 20 customers from all the customers who visited one restaurant location on a particular Friday. Each selected customer is asked whether the customer ordered a vegetarian meal. Which of the following conclusions is best supported by the survey?
choices: The proportion of all residents of the city who ordered a vegetarian meal can be estimated.
Ordering a vegetarian meal causes customers to visit the restaurant more often.
The proportion of customers at that location on that Friday who ordered a vegetarian meal can be estimated.
The proportion of all customers of the restaurant chain who ordered a vegetarian meal can be determined exactly.
items.explanation: Because the sample was randomly selected from customers at that location on that Friday, it can support an estimate for that specific group, but not for all chain customers or city residents.

per_choice.correct: Because the sample was randomly selected from customers at that location on that Friday, it can support an estimate for that specific group, but not for all chain customers or city residents.
per_choice.trap: The distractor claiming the result applies to all chain customers comes from generalizing beyond the population from which the sample was drawn.

items.trap: The distractor claiming the result applies to all chain customers comes from generalizing beyond the population from which the sample was drawn.

items.stem: A fair model predicts that 50% of the items produced by a machine will meet a quality standard. For each sample, an evidence score is calculated as |p - 0.50| / sqrt(0.25/n), where p is the proportion meeting the standard and n is the sample size. Sample A has 52 of 100 items meeting the standard, Sample B has 33 of 50, Sample C has 620 of 1,000, and Sample D has 7 of 10. Which of the following samples has the greatest evidence score?
items.explanation: The evidence scores are approximately 0.40 for Sample A, 2.26 for Sample B, 7.59 for Sample C, and 1.26 for Sample D. Therefore, Sample C has the greatest evidence score. Although Sample D has the percentage farthest from 50%, its sample size is much smaller.
items.pattern: evaluate evidence against a fair model

per_choice.correct: The evidence scores are approximately 0.40 for Sample A, 2.26 for Sample B, 7.59 for Sample C, and 1.26 for Sample D. Therefore, Sample C has the greatest evidence score. Although Sample D has the percentage farthest from 50%, its sample size is much smaller.
per_choice.trap: Choosing Sample D because its observed percentage, 70%, is farthest from 50% ignores the much larger sample size for Sample C.

items.trap: Choosing Sample D because its observed percentage, 70%, is farthest from 50% ignores the much larger sample size for Sample C.

items.stem: A random sample of 240 customers at a store showed that 54 of the customers purchased a certain product. During the same period, the store served 3,200 customers. Assuming the sample is representative of all the customers, which of the following is the best estimate of the number of customers who purchased the product?
items.explanation: The sample proportion is 54/240. Applying this proportion to all 3,200 customers gives (54/240)(3,200) = 720.
items.pattern: extrapolate population count from sample proportion

per_choice.correct: The sample proportion is 54/240. Applying this proportion to all 3,200 customers gives (54/240)(3,200) = 720.
per_choice.trap: Using 54, the number in the sample, as the estimate for the entire population ignores the need to scale the sample proportion to 3,200 customers.

items.trap: Using 54, the number in the sample, as the estimate for the entire population ignores the need to scale the sample proportion to 3,200 customers.

items.stem:
I. Sample III has the largest excess of red classifications over the number expected by the fair model.

II. Sample II provides the strongest evidence of unfairness according to the stated measure.

III. Sample I provides the strongest evidence of unfairness according to the stated measure.
items.stimulus: A quality-control machine is expected to classify red and blue items equally often. Three samples of classifications are recorded. Sample I contains 18 red classifications out of 30, Sample II contains 7 red classifications out of 10, and Sample III contains 55 red classifications out of 100. For this question, the strength of evidence that a sample is unfair is measured by the absolute difference between the observed proportion and 0.5, divided by sqrt(0.25/n), where n is the sample size. Which of the following statements must be true?
items.explanation: The expected numbers of red classifications are 15, 5, and 50 for Samples I, II, and III. Their raw excesses are 3, 2, and 5, so Sample III has the largest raw excess, making I true. The standardized departures are approximately 1.10 for Sample I, 1.26 for Sample II, and 1.00 for Sample III, so Sample II provides the strongest evidence, making II true. Statement III is false.

per_choice.correct: The expected numbers of red classifications are 15, 5, and 50 for Samples I, II, and III. Their raw excesses are 3, 2, and 5, so Sample III has the largest raw excess, making I true. The standardized departures are approximately 1.10 for Sample I, 1.26 for Sample II, and 1.00 for Sample III, so Sample II provides the strongest evidence, making II true. Statement III is false.
per_choice.trap: Choosing Sample III because it has the largest raw excess of red classifications ignores the different sample sizes. Sample II has the largest standardized departure from the fair-model proportion.

items.trap: Choosing Sample III because it has the largest raw excess of red classifications ignores the different sample sizes. Sample II has the largest standardized departure from the fair-model proportion.

items.stem: A researcher wants to estimate the average number of hours students at a large high school sleep. Which sampling method best supports a conclusion about all students at the school?
choices: Surveying the first 50 students who arrive at school
Surveying 50 students chosen at random from the full enrollment list
Surveying 50 students on the varsity sports teams
Surveying 50 students who volunteer to respond online
items.explanation: Only a random sample from the entire population supports a generalization to that population. Each other option systematically over-represents a subgroup: early arrivers, athletes, or volunteers.

per_choice.correct: Only a random sample from the entire population supports a generalization to that population. Each other option systematically over-represents a subgroup: early arrivers, athletes, or volunteers.
per_choice.trap: Choosing the volunteer sample because it is large, even though self-selection biases it.

items.trap: Choosing the volunteer sample because it is large, even though self-selection biases it.

items.stem:
I. For the participating adults, a difference in the mean outcomes of the 2 groups can be attributed to the exercise program rather than to preexisting differences between the groups.

II. The study necessarily estimates the causal effect of the exercise program for all adults in the city.

III. The random selection of adults to invite does not, by itself, ensure that the 320 participants are representative of all adults in the city.
items.stimulus: A public health team randomly selects 500 adults from a complete list of adults in a city and invites them to participate in a study of a new exercise program. Of the adults invited, 320 enroll. The 320 participants are randomly assigned to either use the program or not use it for 8 weeks, and all participants complete the study. Which of the following must be true?
items.explanation: Random assignment supports a causal comparison between the 2 groups of participants, so I must be true. Because 180 invitees did not enroll, the participants may differ systematically from all city adults; therefore III is true, while II is not guaranteed.

per_choice.correct: Random assignment supports a causal comparison between the 2 groups of participants, so I must be true. Because 180 invitees did not enroll, the participants may differ systematically from all city adults; therefore III is true, while II is not guaranteed.
per_choice.trap: Choosing I only treats the random assignment as if it also guaranteed population representativeness; choosing II or II and III confuses random selection of invitees with random sampling of the adults who actually participated.

items.trap: Choosing I only treats the random assignment as if it also guaranteed population representativeness; choosing II or II and III confuses random selection of invitees with random sampling of the adults who actually participated.

items.stem: A transit authority wants to estimate the proportion of all its employees who favor a 4-day workweek. Of the employees, 35% work in maintenance and 65% work in administration. Researchers randomly select 40 maintenance employees and 60 administrative employees, and every selected employee responds. Of the maintenance employees selected, 58% favor the 4-day workweek; of the administrative employees selected, 42% favor it. What is the best estimate of the proportion of all employees who favor the 4-day workweek?
items.explanation: The estimate must weight each sample proportion by that group’s proportion of all employees: 0.35(0.58) + 0.65(0.42) = 0.476, or 47.6%. The sample’s 40%-60% group split should not be used because it does not match the employee population.

per_choice.correct: The estimate must weight each sample proportion by that group’s proportion of all employees: 0.35(0.58) + 0.65(0.42) = 0.476, or 47.6%. The sample’s 40%-60% group split should not be used because it does not match the employee population.
per_choice.trap: Using the sample’s group proportions instead of the population proportions gives 0.40(0.58) + 0.60(0.42) = 48.4%; averaging the 2 sample percentages gives 50%.

items.trap: Using the sample’s group proportions instead of the population proportions gives 0.40(0.58) + 0.60(0.42) = 48.4%; averaging the 2 sample percentages gives 50%.

items.stem:
I. Each household on the list had the same probability of being selected.

II. The sample can support a conclusion about households with broadband subscriptions.

III. The sample necessarily supports a conclusion about all households in the county.
items.stimulus: A county maintains a complete list of households that have a broadband subscription. A researcher randomly selects households from this list to survey about transportation habits, and every selected household responds. The researcher wants to draw conclusions about households with broadband subscriptions and also about all households in the county. Which of the following statements must be true?
items.explanation: A random sample from the list gives each listed household the same selection probability and supports inference about the population represented by that list. Because households without broadband are not on the list, the sample does not necessarily represent all county households.

per_choice.correct: A random sample from the list gives each listed household the same selection probability and supports inference about the population represented by that list. Because households without broadband are not on the list, the sample does not necessarily represent all county households.
per_choice.trap: Treating a random sample from a sampling frame as a random sample of the entire target population incorrectly makes III seem true.

items.trap: Treating a random sample from a sampling frame as a random sample of the entire target population incorrectly makes III seem true.

items.stem: A health department randomly selects 1,000 adults from a complete list of adults in a city, and all selected adults respond. Each adult reports whether the adult regularly uses a fitness tracker and whether the adult met a weekly activity guideline. Among the fitness-tracker users, 38% met the guideline; among the nonusers, 22% met it. All of the following conclusions are supported by the information given EXCEPT:
choices: In the sample, fitness-tracker users had a higher observed rate of meeting the guideline than nonusers.
If the sample is representative, the difference in these rates can be used to estimate the association between fitness-tracker use and meeting the guideline for all adults in the city.
Regularly using a fitness tracker causes an adult to be more likely to meet the guideline.
The study does not, by itself, establish that fitness-tracker use causes adults to be more likely to meet the guideline.
items.explanation: The random sample supports generalizing the observed association to the city’s adults if the sample is representative. However, fitness-tracker use was not randomly assigned, so the comparison cannot establish a causal effect.

per_choice.correct: The random sample supports generalizing the observed association to the city’s adults if the sample is representative. However, fitness-tracker use was not randomly assigned, so the comparison cannot establish a causal effect.
per_choice.trap: Confusing random selection of adults with random assignment to use a fitness tracker produces the unsupported causal conclusion.

items.trap: Confusing random selection of adults with random assignment to use a fitness tracker produces the unsupported causal conclusion.

items.stem:
I. Within each age group, every person had the same probability of being selected.
II. Adults make up 50% of the sample, even though they make up 70% of the county's population.
III. The unweighted combined proportion is not generally an appropriate estimate of the proportion for all county residents.
items.stimulus: A county's residents are 70% adults and 30% teenagers. To estimate the proportion of all residents who favor a proposed measure, a researcher randomly selects 100 adults and independently randomly selects 100 teenagers. Every person selected responds. The researcher combines the 200 responses without weighting the 2 groups. Which of the following statements must be true?
items.explanation: Random selection within each age group gives equal selection probability within that group, and the equal sample sizes make adults 50% of the sample. Because the county's age groups are not equal in size, the two groups should generally be weighted differently when estimating the countywide proportion.

per_choice.correct: Random selection within each age group gives equal selection probability within that group, and the equal sample sizes make adults 50% of the sample. Because the county's age groups are not equal in size, the two groups should generally be weighted differently when estimating the countywide proportion.
per_choice.trap: Treating equal sample sizes from the 2 groups as representative of their unequal population sizes leads to the distractor 'I and II only,' because it overlooks the need for weighting; ignoring the stated random sampling within groups can lead to 'II and III only.'

items.trap: Treating equal sample sizes from the 2 groups as representative of their unequal population sizes leads to the distractor 'I and II only,' because it overlooks the need for weighting; ignoring the stated random sampling within groups can lead to 'II and III only.'

items.stem:
I. The poll is a voluntary-response sample.
II. The 68% describes the proportion of the respondents who reported exercising at least 3 times per week.
III. The poll result alone cannot justify concluding that 68% of all magazine readers exercise at least 3 times per week.
items.stimulus: A magazine places an online poll at the end of an article about exercise. Of the readers who choose to respond, 68% report exercising at least 3 times per week. The magazine receives 2,000 responses. Which of the following statements must be true?
items.explanation: Readers decide for themselves whether to participate, so the sample is voluntary-response, and 68% is a descriptive result for those respondents. A large number of voluntary responses does not by itself make the sample representative of all readers, so the population conclusion is unsupported by the poll alone.

per_choice.correct: Readers decide for themselves whether to participate, so the sample is voluntary-response, and 68% is a descriptive result for those respondents. A large number of voluntary responses does not by itself make the sample representative of all readers, so the population conclusion is unsupported by the poll alone.
per_choice.trap: Assuming that 2,000 responses eliminate selection bias produces 'I and II only'; treating the 68% as a population percentage rather than a respondent percentage produces 'II only.'

items.trap: Assuming that 2,000 responses eliminate selection bias produces 'I and II only'; treating the 68% as a population percentage rather than a respondent percentage produces 'II only.'

items.stem:
I. The difference in mean weekly viewing time can be used to estimate the difference between the 2 interfaces for the population of current subscribers.
II. For the subscribers in the study, a difference in mean viewing time can be attributed to the interfaces rather than to preexisting differences between the 2 assigned groups.
III. The study necessarily establishes that the same causal effect will occur for people who are not current subscribers.
items.stimulus: A streaming service randomly selects 600 current subscribers from its complete subscriber list. It randomly assigns 300 of these subscribers to use recommendation interface A and 300 to use recommendation interface B for 1 month, then compares their mean weekly viewing times. Assume that all 600 subscribers complete the study. Which of the following statements must be true?
items.explanation: Random selection from the complete list supports generalizing the comparison to current subscribers, while random assignment supports a causal interpretation for the subscribers in the experiment. Neither procedure supports applying the causal conclusion necessarily to non-subscribers, who were not part of the sampled population.

per_choice.correct: Random selection from the complete list supports generalizing the comparison to current subscribers, while random assignment supports a causal interpretation for the subscribers in the experiment. Neither procedure supports applying the causal conclusion necessarily to non-subscribers, who were not part of the sampled population.
per_choice.trap: Confusing random assignment with random selection leads to 'II only,' while assuming that a randomly selected subscriber sample represents every type of potential user leads to 'I and III only.'

items.trap: Confusing random assignment with random selection leads to 'II only,' while assuming that a randomly selected subscriber sample represents every type of potential user leads to 'I and III only.'
